'''Washington Mio''' is a mathematician specializing in [[geometric topology]] and [[Shape analysis (digital geometry)|shape analysis]]. He is a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] and served as the chair of [[Florida State University]]'s mathematics department.

==Career==
Mio earned his bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[State University of Campinas]], Brazil in 1978. Two years later he finished his M.S. in mathematics from the [[Instituto Nacional de Matemática Pura e Aplicada|Instituto de Matemática Pura e Aplicada]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mio |first1=Washington |title=Short CV |url=https://www.math.fsu.edu/~mio/mio-shortcv-25}}</ref> Mio completed his Ph.D. at [[New York University]] in 1984 with [[Sylvain Cappell]] as his advisor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Washington Mio - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=33812 |website=www.mathgenealogy.org |access-date=20 July 2025 |archive-date=29 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240829010922/https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=33812 |url-status=live }}</ref> His dissertation was published in the [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mio |first1=Washington |title=Nonlinearly Equivalent Representations of Quaternionic 2-Groups |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |date=September 1989 |volume=315 |issue=1 |pages=305–321 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1989-315-01/S0002-9947-1989-0937879-0/S0002-9947-1989-0937879-0.pdf |publisher=American Mathematical Society |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1989-0937879-0 }}</ref>

In 1996 Mio, along with John Bryant, Steven Ferry, and [[Shmuel Weinberger]], disproved [[James W. Cannon|James Cannon]]'s influential ''Resolution Conjecture'' using [[surgery theory]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bryant |first1=J. |last2=Ferry |first2=S. |last3=Mio |first3=W. |last4=Weinberger |first4=S. |title=Topology of Homology Manifolds |journal=Annals of Mathematics |date=1996 |volume=143 |issue=3 |pages=435–467 |doi=10.2307/2118532 |jstor=2118532 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2118532 |issn=0003-486X |archive-date=2024-02-05 |access-date=2025-07-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240205004733/https://www.jstor.org/stable/2118532 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2004 Mio, together with Eric Klassen, Anuj Srivastava, and Shantanu H. Joshi, introduced a widely used method for analyzing and automatically classifying shapes based on [[geodesic|geodesic paths]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klassen |first1=E. |last2=Srivastava |first2=A. |last3=Mio |first3=M. |last4=Joshi |first4=S.H. |title=Analysis of planar shapes using geodesic paths on shape spaces |journal=IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence |date=March 2004 |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=372–383 |doi=10.1109/TPAMI.2004.1262333 |pmid=15376883 |bibcode=2004ITPAM..26..372K |issn=1939-3539}}</ref>

==Awards==
In 2015, Mio was inducted as a [[fellow of the American Mathematical Society]] for "contributions to topology as well as to the mathematics, statistics, and applications of shape analysis."<ref>{{Cite journal |date=March 2015 |title=2015 Class of the Fellows of the AMS |url=https://www.ams.org/grants-awards/ams-fellows/rnoti-p285.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=285–287 |access-date=20 July 2025 |archive-date=18 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250218053550/http://www.ams.org/grants-awards/ams-fellows/rnoti-p285.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Florida State University]] awarded Mio the title of Distinguished Research Professor in 2023<ref>{{cite web |title=Faculty Honors & Awards |url=https://awards.faculty.fsu.edu/honorees/ |website=awards.faculty.fsu.edu |access-date=20 July 2025 |archive-date=12 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250512023711/https://awards.faculty.fsu.edu/honorees/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and made him the inaugural Roger W. Roberts Professor of Mathematics in 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=Department of Mathematics Newsletter |url=https://www.math.fsu.edu/Newsletter/2024_Math_Newsletter.pdf |page=11 |date=March 2024 |access-date=2025-07-20 |archive-date=2025-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250426003128/https://www.math.fsu.edu/Newsletter/2024_Math_Newsletter.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>
